Measure theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis Real analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 23k Articles: 390
Measure theory studies measures, which assign sizes to measurable sets, and the Lebesgue integral, which accumulates values weighted by those sizes. The same framework describes Lebesgue measure on the real numbers, counting measure on discrete collections, and probability measures on possible outcomes. The choice of measure determines what counts as large; the choice of sigma-algebra determines what can be measured.
A striking example separates size from proximity: the rational numbers in [0,1] form a dense set with Lebesgue measure zero, although the whole interval has Lebesgue measure one. This distinction makes almost everywhere statements useful: exceptional null sets can be ignored in a Lebesgue integral even when they meet every open subinterval. The monotone convergence theorem and dominated convergence theorem then give precise conditions for passing a limit through an integral.
A historical starting point is Lebesgue's 1902 thesis, [ref]. Its title connects integration with the geometric task of assigning sizes.

Convergence in measure (μ(∣fn​−f∣>ε)→0(ε>0))

Words: 209 Articles: 1
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A sequence of real measurable functions converges in measure to f when the displayed condition holds for every positive threshold. It controls the measure of the exceptional set at each index, rather than requiring eventual closeness on each sample path. On a probability space it is exactly convergence in probability. On a finite measure space, almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure by continuity of measure on the decreasing tail events. The converse need not hold for the full sequence, but convergence in measure always admits an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence.

Completeness of convergence in measure on a finite measure space (d(f,g)=∫min{1,∣f−g∣}dμ,μ(E)<∞)

Words: 124
Convergence in measure OurBigBook.com
Modulo equality almost everywhere, the displayed metric induces convergence in measure and is complete. A sequence Cauchy in measure has a strictly increasing subsequence fnk​​ with μ(∣fnk+1​​−fnk​​∣>2−k)<2−k. Subadditivity makes the limsup of these exceptional sets null, so the subsequence has summable pointwise successive differences almost everywhere. It therefore has a finite measurable limit. Almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure for finite measure, and the triangle inequality plus the original Cauchy property extends convergence to the full sequence.
For the metric equivalence, d(fn​,f)≤εμ(E)+μ(∣fn​−f∣>ε) for 0<ε<1, while μ(∣fn​−f∣>ε)≤d(fn​,f)/min{1,ε}. The same estimates compare the two Cauchy properties. Define the subsequence limit as zero where no finite limit exists; that exceptional set is measurable by the countable Cauchy criterion, so completeness of the underlying measure is unnecessary.

Non-measurable set (A∈/Σ)

Words: 124
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A subset A of a measurable space (X,Σ) is non-measurable when A∈/Σ. On the real line, unless another sigma-algebra is specified, this commonly means that A is not a Lebesgue measurable set. By completeness of Lebesgue measure, such a set cannot be contained in a Lebesgue null set.
For an example, use the axiom of choice to select one representative from each equivalence class of [0,1] under x∼y if x−y∈Q, and call the resulting set V. The translates V+q, for q∈Q∩[−1,1], are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1], and their union is contained in [−1,2]. If V were a Lebesgue measurable set, translation invariance and countable additivity would make that union have measure zero when m(V)=0 and infinite measure when m(V)>0. Both conclusions contradict these inclusions. Thus V is non-measurable.

Wiener covering lemma

Words: 133 Articles: 1
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A finite collection of Euclidean open balls has a disjoint subcollection whose concentric triples cover the original union. Greedily retain a largest remaining ball and discard all intersecting ones. Each discarded ball has radius no greater than the retained one and lies in its triple. Lebesgue measure consequently bounds the original union by 3d times the sum of the retained volumes. This covering lemma is distinct from inverse-closedness results for the Wiener algebra.

Disjoint ball decomposition modulo null sets

Words: 63
Wiener covering lemma OurBigBook.com
Every open set of finite Lebesgue measure in Euclidean space is covered, up to a null set, by countably many pairwise disjoint open balls contained in it. At each stage cover a compact subset of the open remainder, choose a packing with the Wiener covering lemma, and remove its closed balls. A fixed positive fraction of the remaining measure is removed each time, while sphere boundaries are null.

Geometric measure theory

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
Geometric measure theory uses measures and analysis to study geometric objects that need not be smooth. Its measuring rules can distinguish a curve from its surrounding plane or capture the fine structure of a fractal. Hausdorff measure supplies size adapted to an exponent, while Hausdorff dimension identifies the exponent at which that size changes character.
The Cantor set is an elementary starting point: it has zero Lebesgue measure but positive Hausdorff dimension. In Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set, explicit small covers give an upper bound and a distributed probability measure supplies the matching lower bound. This combination of geometric coverings and analytic control is useful even before more advanced tools for irregular surfaces are introduced.

Coarea formula (∫g∣∇Φ∣dx=∫R​∫Φ−1(s)​gdSds)

Words: 69
Geometric measure theory OurBigBook.com
For a scalar smooth map Φ:Rn→R, integration can be decomposed into its level surfaces with the gradient weight displayed in the title. Near a regular level, using Φ as the normal coordinate gives the volume element dx=dSds/∣∇Φ∣, which explains the formula by integration by substitution. In particular, ∫W(x)δ(Φ(x))dx=∫Φ=0​W/∣∇Φ∣dS when the zero level is regular and the integrals are well-defined. General versions allow Lipschitz functions and maps into higher-dimensional spaces.

Hausdorff measure (Hs)

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Geometric measure theory OurBigBook.com
Hausdorff measure measures the geometric size of a set using covers by increasingly small pieces. The exponent s chooses the measuring scale: s=1 is length-like, s=2 is area-like, and noninteger exponents can measure fractals. Unlike a count of occupied grid cells, the construction allows pieces of different sizes and considers every admissible cover.
For s>0 and a subset E of a metric space, use the diameter-cost convention
Hδs​(E)=inf{∑j=1∞​(diamUj​)s:E⊆⋃j​Uj​,diamUj​≤δ},Hs(E)=limδ↓0​Hδs​(E).
(1)
The first quantity is scale-restricted Hausdorff content. Shrinking δ removes options from the infimum, so these contents increase to a limit, possibly infinite. The resulting outer measure restricts to a measure on the Borel sets. For s=0, counting each nonempty covering piece with cost one gives counting measure.
A different common convention multiplies these quantities by cs​=πs/2/(2sΓ(1+s/2)), using the Gamma function. At integer s, that normalization agrees with ordinary Euclidean s-dimensional volume. Here c1​=1, so both conventions make H1 agree with arc length on smooth curves in Euclidean space. Positive normalization constants never change Hausdorff dimension. A definition must specify this constant when numerical values of Hausdorff measure matter.
For a line segment of length L, splitting it into n equal pieces gives the cover cost
n(L/n)s=Lsn1−s.
(2)
It tends to zero for s>1, stays at L for s=1, and grows for s<1. The matching lower bound comes from the fact that any interval cover must have total length at least L. The exponent one is therefore the transition between a measuring rule too coarse to see the segment and one that assigns it infinite size. For a Cantor set, the transition is instead at log2/log3, as shown in Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set.
This makes Hausdorff measure useful when ordinary Lebesgue measure sees too little: a curve in the plane has zero planar area but can have positive arc length, and the Cantor set has zero line length but positive geometric size at its own dimension. It also separates local covering estimates from global cardinality: a countable dense set has zero Hausdorff dimension, despite meeting every open region of its closure.
An original source for the construction is Felix Hausdorff's [ref]. The modern covering and Hausdorff dimension framework is developed in Bishop and Peres, Fractals in Probability and Analysis, §1.2.

Scale-restricted Hausdorff content (Hδs​(F))

Words: 104
Hausdorff measure OurBigBook.com
For δ>0, scale-restricted Hausdorff content is the infimum of ∑j​(diamUj​)s over countable covers of F by sets of diameter at most δ, using the convention in Hausdorff measure. It increases as δ decreases; its limit is Hausdorff measure. Unrestricted Hausdorff content imposes no diameter bound and can behave differently.
Any explicit cover supplies an upper bound on scale-restricted Hausdorff content, rather than its exact value. The level-n intervals of the Cantor set, for example, give
H3−ns​(C)≤2n3−ns.
(3)
If this right-hand side tends to zero, then Hs(C)=0. If it grows, that alone proves no positive lower bound: a different cover might be cheaper. The mass distribution principle addresses precisely this gap by bounding the cost of every sufficiently small cover.

Hausdorff dimension (dimH​E)

Words: 760 Articles: 4
Hausdorff measure OurBigBook.com
The Hausdorff dimension is the critical exponent at which Hausdorff measure changes from infinite to zero:
dimH​E=inf{s≥0:Hs(E)=0}=sup{s≥0:Hs(E)=∞},
(4)
with the standard endpoint convention for an empty supremum. This measures fine-scale geometric size rather than the number of coordinates used to describe the set. A line segment has Hausdorff dimension one; a square has dimension two; the middle-third Cantor set has dimension log2/log3≈0.63093.
Why can a dimension be fractional? At a scale reduced by a factor of three, the Cantor set needs twice as many construction intervals. The balance 2(1/3)d=1 gives d=log2/log3, between the growth rates of finitely many points and a whole interval. Making this argument rigorous requires a cover upper bound and the mass distribution principle lower bound, as in Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set.
At the critical exponent itself, Hausdorff measure can be zero, finite and positive, or infinite; dimension does not specify that endpoint value. For example, finite sets and countably infinite sets both have dimension zero, although their counting measures differ. Dimension is also different from a finite-resolution estimate: box-counting dimension is another asymptotic definition, and fitting a scaling slope over a handful of observed scales does not establish either dimension.
The metric matters. Multiplying every distance by a fixed positive constant multiplies Hs by that constant to the power s and preserves Hausdorff dimension. A Lipschitz map cannot increase it, because mapped cover diameters increase by at most a fixed factor. A bi-Lipschitz map therefore preserves it by applying this fact in both directions. These properties make Hausdorff dimension useful for comparing geometric models while controlling how their measurements change.

Words: 148
Hausdorff dimension OurBigBook.com
The mass distribution principle converts a diffuse measure into a lower bound on Hausdorff dimension. Let s>0 and let a Borel probability measure μ give a Borel set E full mass. If, for some C,r0​>0, every ball centered in E satisfies
μ(B(x,r))≤Crs(0<r<r0​),
(5)
then Hs(E)≥1/C>0 in the diameter-cost convention, and consequently dimH​E≥s.
The idea is to keep unit mass from being crowded into cheap covering pieces. For a piece U of positive diameter r meeting E, choose x∈U∩E. A ball of radius r+ε contains U; letting ε↓0 gives μ∗(U)≤Crs, where μ∗ is the associated outer measure. Zero-diameter pieces have zero mass by the same estimate. For any sufficiently small cover,
1=μ(E)≤∑j​μ∗(Uj​)≤C∑j​(diamUj​)s.
(6)
Thus every cover costs at least 1/C. This is the lower-bound counterpart to the explicit covers in scale-restricted Hausdorff content. The Cantor distribution supplies the needed mass in Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set. [ref].

Hausdorff dimension OurBigBook.com
The middle-third Cantor set has Hausdorff dimension
d=log3log2​≈0.63093.
(7)
Its Lebesgue measure is zero, yet 0<Hd(C)<∞. These assertions measure different aspects of size: interval length is too coarse to distinguish this set from a null set, while the critical fractional measuring rule captures its remaining structure.
At level n, the construction covers C by 2n intervals of diameter 3−n. Their total s-cost is
2n(3−n)s=(23−s)n.
(8)
For s>d it tends to zero, proving the upper dimension bound. At s=d it equals one, giving Hd(C)≤1. For s<d this particular cover's cost grows, but that alone would not prove a lower bound on Hausdorff measure.
For the matching lower bound, use the Cantor distribution, which assigns mass 2−n to each level-n Cantor cylinder. An interval of length r with 3−(n+1)<r≤3−n meets at most two level-n construction intervals, since their gaps are at least 3−n. Its mass is therefore at most
22−n=2(3−n)d<23drd=4rd.
(9)
Every covering set of diameter r in the line lies in an interval of length r, so any small cover must have total d-cost at least 1/4. This is the mass distribution principle in its interval form: 1/4≤Hd(C)≤1, sufficient to prove the claimed dimension. The constants are convenient bounds, rather than an assertion of the exact critical Hausdorff measure. In the diagram, the right panel is a finite-stage approximation to the Cantor function, showing how probability is shared while the middle third receives none.
The reusable pattern is to obtain an upper bound by constructing covers and a lower bound by distributing mass. The same strategy underlies Cartesian powers of the Cantor set and the dimension formula for a finite similarity iterated function system satisfying the open set condition.

The Lipschitz map x↦∣x−a∣ maps C onto a set containing [0,∣b−a∣], since continuous images of connected spaces are connected. A Lipschitz map cannot increase Hausdorff dimension, whereas an interval has Hausdorff dimension one. Consequently any set of Hausdorff dimension less than one is totally disconnected.

Each level set is X−1(B) for a Borel set B, so each approximation factors as Zm​=gm​(X) with gm​ a Borel measurable function. Essential range (essranμ​m)

Words: 455
Measurable function OurBigBook.com
The essential range of a real or complex measurable function m consists of the values z whose every neighborhood receives inputs of positive measure:
essranμ​m={z:μ({x:∣m(x)−z∣<ε})>0 for every ε>0}.
(12)
It depends on the measure as well as the function. This definition concerns values arbitrarily near z, not necessarily inputs at which m=z exactly. It therefore retains meaningful limiting values while ignoring values occurring only on null sets. [ref].
For m(x)=x on (0,1) with Lebesgue measure, the ordinary image of a function is (0,1), but the essential range is [0,1]. Neither endpoint is attained, yet inputs with ∣m(x)∣<ε or ∣m(x)−1∣<ε have positive measure for every ε>0. Every interior value also belongs to the essential range, although its exact fiber is a singleton of zero measure. Positive measure of a fiber is sufficient, but is not necessary, for a value to belong to the essential range.
The two-sided example g from essential infimum and essential supremum illustrates what disappears. It follows g(x)=x on [0,1], except g(1/4)=−3 and g(3/4)=4. Its ordinary image of a function is ([0,1]∖{1/4,3/4})∪{−3,4}, whereas its essential range remains [0,1]. The missing ordinary values 1/4 and 3/4 still have arbitrarily close neighbors with positive measure; the exceptional values −3 and 4 can each be isolated by a sufficiently small neighborhood whose preimage is a null set.
For the three-point example in L-infinity norm, the values are 1,3,10. With weights (0.5,0.5,0) the essential range is {1,3}; with weights (0.499,0.5,0.001) it is {1,3,10}. A small but positive probability retains ten, so an essential range does not discard a value merely because it is rare. For a real function on a space of positive total measure, the essential infimum and essential supremum are the lower and upper edges of its essential range, allowing infinite bounds. The L-infinity norm instead takes the upper edge of the essential range of ∣m∣.
A useful operator connection is the spectrum of a real multiplication operator: on a nonzero L2 space over a sigma-finite measure, multiplication by a real measurable function m has spectrum equal to its essential range, with the natural domain when m is unbounded. Outside that range, ∣m−z∣ has a positive lower bound almost everywhere, so multiplication by 1/(m−z) gives an inverse function that is a bounded linear operator. Near an essential value, this lower bound fails. Thus discarding null sets is precisely what makes the range match an operator acting on almost everywhere equivalence classes. [ref].

Approximation proves the displayed almost everywhere assertion. Refinement supplies the maximal estimate; shrinking diameter supplies the approximation argument. Without shrinking diameter, a constant partition generally converges only to its cell averages.

The law of total expectation makes averaging in stages reliable, provided the outer stage uses the actual probabilities of the groups. For an integrable random variable X and a sub-sigma-algebra G,

For a complete finite example, choose a group Y=A with probability 1/4 and Y=B with probability 3/4. Within group A, X is 0 or 4 with equal conditional probabilities; within group B, it is 6 or 10 with equal conditional probabilities. Thus the joint probability distribution puts probabilities 1/8,1/8,3/8,3/8 on (A,0),(A,4),(B,6),(B,10). The conditional means are two and eight. Consequently,
EX=41​⋅2+43​⋅8=213​.​

The formula is useful when conditioning on a first choice makes the remaining experiment simple. It can replace a large outcome enumeration by smaller calculations within groups. In a mixture distribution, it combines component means using mixture weights; in a random sum of independent claims, it separates the number of summands from their individual expected values under the stated independence assumptions. The same averaging step appears in the law of total variance.

Outer measure

Words: 644 Articles: 10
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
An outer measure μ∗ is defined on every subset, vanishes on the empty set, is monotone, and is countably subadditive.

Metric outer measure (d(A,B)>0⟹μ∗(A∪B)=μ∗(A)+μ∗(B))

Words: 67
Outer measure OurBigBook.com
An outer measure on a metric space is metric when positively separated sets satisfy the displayed equality. Every Borel set is then measurable under Caratheodory measurability criterion. Lebesgue outer measure is metric: refine every box of a covering into finitely many boxes of diameter smaller than the separation. Each refined box meets at most one of the two sets, splitting the cover without changing its total volume. Taking infima proves the additive lower bound; outer subadditivity gives equality.

Regular outer measure (∀A ∃G⊇A:G measurable,μ∗(G)=μ∗(A))

Words: 240 Articles: 2
Outer measure OurBigBook.com
An outer measure is regular in this sense when every set admits a measurable hull of equal outer measure. This is different from merely specifying inner or outer approximation of already measurable sets by compact or open sets. Lebesgue outer measure has a hull that is a Borel set: for finite outer measure choose open covers of total volumes within 1/j of its value and intersect their unions. Monotonicity gives equality of the hull's outer measure with that of the original set. For infinite outer measure the whole Euclidean space is a hull. This regularity is useful for turning numerical equality of inner and outer sizes into measurability.

Words: 71
Regular outer measure OurBigBook.com
For a regular outer measure, its Caratheodory measurability criterion defines a maximal algebra of sets on which that outer measure is finitely additive. Indeed, suppose an additive algebra contains all measurable sets and also A. Given E of finite outer measure, take a measurable hull H⊇E of equal mass. Finite additivity splits H by A, and monotonicity gives μ∗(E)≥μ∗(E∩A)+μ∗(E∖A). Outer subadditivity gives equality. For infinite mass that equality already follows from outer subadditivity. Thus A was measurable. No sigma-finite measure assumption is necessary.

For a regular outer measure and measurable M, the forward implication is countable additivity. For the reverse, choose a measurable hull of A and intersect it with M to obtain A⊆B⊆M and μ(B)=μ∗(A). Measurability of B splits M∖A into M∖B and B∖A, so
μ∗(M∖A)=μ(M∖B)+μ∗(B∖A).
(38)
The assumed equality and finiteness force μ∗(B∖A)=0. Every outer-measure-null set is measurable by Caratheodory measurability criterion, so A=B∖(B∖A) is measurable. Finiteness prevents invalid subtraction of infinite masses.

No measurability assumption on the An​ is needed.

A step function is constant on each member of a finite or countable measurable partition of its domain. Indicator functions of measurable sets are basic examples.

A continuous function on a compact interval is uniformly continuous by the Heine-Cantor theorem. Choose a partition of an interval whose widths lie below the input tolerance for a desired output error ε. On each half-open partition subinterval, use the value of the function at its left endpoint, and assign the rightmost endpoint its own value. This defines a step function whose error is strictly below ε at every input. Finitely assigned partition-point values are allowed and do not alter the Riemann integral.

For a nonnegative measurable function f:X→[0,∞] on a measure space, define
∫X​fdμ=sup{∫X​sdμ:s is a nonnegative simple function, 0≤s≤f}.
(42)
The supremum may be infinite. A simple function assigns finitely many heights to measurable sets, so its integral is height times measure, summed over those pieces. This definition groups points by their values rather than requiring a partition into short intervals. See MIT lecture 11, Definition 108.
A real-valued function is Lebesgue integrable when ∫X​∣f∣dμ<∞. Its integral is ∫X​f+​dμ−∫X​f−​dμ, where f+​=max(f,0) is its positive part and f−​=max(−f,0). This finiteness requirement avoids subtracting two infinities. For functions taking values in the complex numbers, integrate the real part and imaginary part separately.
Consider the Dirichlet function f=1Q∩[0,1]​ on [0,1]. It is a simple function, and
∫[0,1]​fdλ=λ(Q∩[0,1])=0.
(43)
Its Riemann integral does not exist. For every partition of an interval 0=x0​<⋯<xn​=1, each nondegenerate [xi−1​,xi​] contains both rational numbers and irrational numbers, by their respective density of the rational numbers and density of the irrational numbers. Thus its infimum there is 0 and its supremum is 1. The lower Darboux sum is ∑i​0(xi​−xi−1​)=0, whereas the upper Darboux sum is ∑i​1(xi​−xi−1​)=1. Refinement never closes this gap. A finite scatterplot cannot represent this behavior: the assertion concerns every subinterval and every partition of an interval.
Another view builds the Lebesgue integral from horizontal layers. For any nonnegative measurable function, the layer cake representation states
∫X​fdμ=∫0∞​μ({x∈X:f(x)>t})dt.
(44)
Both sides may be infinite. The right side integrates the measure of a superlevel set against Lebesgue measure in the height variable t. See Gautam Iyer's measure theory notes, Theorem 9.5.
For f(x)=x2 on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, the superlevel set at 0≤t<1 is (t​,1], of Lebesgue measure 1−t​; for t≥1 it is empty. Consequently
∫01​x2dλ(x)=∫01​(1−t​)dt=[t−32​t3/2]01​=31​.
(45)
At height t=1/4, the layer extends from x=1/2 to x=1, a width of 1/2. The picture shows why the same area can be accumulated vertically or horizontally. In a probability space, the identical formula expresses the expected value of a nonnegative random variable through its exceedance probabilities.
A proof outline avoids extra assumptions on the measure space. For a nonnegative simple function s=∑j​aj​1Aj​​ with disjoint measurable sets Aj​, the superlevel set has measure ∑aj​>t​μ(Aj​). The full Lebesgue measure is the completion of a measure of this restriction; its domain is the Lebesgue measurable sets. Translation invariance follows by comparing a translated Borel measure on half-open intervals and applying the uniqueness theorem for measures. For the construction and interval properties, see MIT lecture 8.

Thus a dense set can be a null set, and a union of null sets indexed by an uncountable set can have positive Lebesgue measure. The distinction explains both the Dirichlet function example and why almost everywhere is weaker than everywhere.

If fn​→f in Lp for 1≤p<∞, choose a subsequence with ∥fnk​​−f∥pp​≤2−k. Tonelli's theorem makes ∑k​∣fnk​​−f∣p finite almost everywhere, so fnk​​→f almost everywhere. For p=∞, norm convergence itself gives almost-everywhere convergence after removing one common null set.

Lq inclusion implies finite measure on a Euclidean Borel subset

Words: 36
Lp inclusion on a finite measure space OurBigBook.com
Let X⊆Rn be Borel. If Lq(X)⊆Lp(X) for 1≤p<q≤∞, the closed graph theorem makes the inclusion continuous. Applying its norm bound to indicators of X∩B(0,R) shows that their measures are uniformly bounded, hence μ(X)<∞.

Power singularity integrability

Words: 17
Lp inclusion on a finite measure space OurBigBook.com
On (0,1), x−a is integrable exactly when a<1, providing sharp counterexamples between finite-measure Lp spaces.
